TL;DR

A CPU-only ML system, with testable decisions.

FastAPI + PostgreSQL/pgvector; YuNet + SFace for 1:N identification; a separate ONNX Runtime + OCR document service. Deployed to a test environment. v1.3.0-rc.3 is a supervised institutional pilot candidate.

Current recognition benchmark: p95 74 ms with one identification, 1.87 s with 20. Document classification: F1 0.778 on a 297/64/64 split. These measure different tasks; historical diagnostics use other splits.

Limits: institutional calibration and operational approval pending; small document test; one environment for load benchmarks; sample FAR=0 is not evidence of zero risk.

Unplanned finding

Two simultaneous clock-ins caused 6 out of 6 extraction failures.

Detector and recognizer shared state: 8 punches caused 24 failures. I serialized access and added a regression test with 8 threads × 3 frames.

Notebooks 15–18 and ml/face_bench.py reproduce extraction, normalization, and thresholds.

Classification experiment

A ladder of baselines, from trivial to hybrid.

I compared trivial, classical, neural, and hybrid classifiers under the same selection and test protocol.

Separate service: 297 training, 64 validation, and 64 test documents in a versioned stratified split. The test set was excluded from selection.

Grid search with five-fold stratified validation optimized medical-document F1. The majority baseline has 68.8% accuracy and zero F1; the held-out test supports this comparison only.

Wilson 95% intervals and paired-test limit

From the notebooks' aggregate counts, in table order (accuracy / precision / recall): floor 0.566–0.788 / undefined / 0–0.161; HOG linear 0.632–0.840 / 0.388–0.755 / 0.481–0.855; HOG RBF 0.683–0.877 / 0.480–0.891 / 0.342–0.742; original head 0.649–0.853 / 0.408–0.778 / 0.481–0.855; hybrid 0.772–0.935 / 0.640–0.965 / 0.481–0.855. Per-document predictions are unavailable in the versioned artifacts, so paired McNemar is not reported.

0.778 F1 for the certificate class of the winning solution: EfficientNet as an embedding extractor + Logistic Regression
0.875 accuracy of the hybrid solution on the held-out test set, above the network’s original head (0.766)
−7 false positives relative to the original neural head, preserving the same recall of 0.700

HOG + SVM reached F1 0.636, below the original neural head (0.651). The selected solution combines EfficientNet’s 1,280-dimensional embeddings with Logistic Regression. OCR provides rule-based review.

Both heads detect 14 of 20 medical documents: 6 false negatives each. False positives fall from 9 to 2; accuracy is 49/64 versus 56/64. ROC AUC from 0.814 to 0.892 and PR AUC from 0.697 to 0.823 indicate better observed ranking; they do not choose the operational threshold by themselves.

With 64 test documents, one error changes accuracy by 1.56 points; small validation differences do not justify ranking embedding classifiers.

Investigation method

Measure before concluding.

Inspect orientation and paired comparisons

I investigated OCR failures and identified images loaded with incorrect orientation.

468 documents triaged automatically using objective quality signals
38 images reached the model rotated because of an ignored EXIF metadata tag
2,071 lines removed after concluding that an experiment’s premise did not hold
  • EXIF orientation: the pipeline ignored the Orientation tag and sent rotated documents to the network and OCR; normalization is now centralized at loading.
  • Hypothesis validation: the orientation detector flagged 45% of the data; 91 of 109 “180°” cases were screenshots. EXIF metadata distinguished actual rotation from detector noise.
  • Training/inference consistency: I centralized normalization in image loading and the training loader to avoid train/serve skew. After retraining, the classifier effect was neutral.
  • Paired metrics: I rejected Jensen-Shannon after demonstrating zero marginal divergence in a case with 100% document-level disagreement. I adopted document-by-document comparisons.

Experimental diagnosis

Hypotheses evaluated through experiments.

Read historical hypotheses and ablations

I investigated the classifier’s limited learning through controlled experiments, changing one variable at a time.

3 hypotheses investigated; results weakened initial explanations within the tested protocol
4 epochs for the same parameters to fit a subset, indicating ability to memorize that subset
+16 percentage points gained in historical validation; successive changes do not isolate interactions
  • Capacity: without regularization, the same parameters fit a subset in four epochs. The test showed the network could memorize this subset; it does not measure generalization.
  • Label smoothing: removing it did not raise the observed confidence ceiling, ruling out the initial hypothesis.
  • Threshold: I simulated the pipeline across nine values. Lower thresholds improved the isolated classifier but worsened the final result by favoring the less accurate component.
  • Augmentation: removing horizontal flipping alone had no effect. Reducing the total transformation load raised validation accuracy by thirteen percentage points and extended learning from four to twenty-three epochs.
  • Early stopping: accuracy saturated on the small validation set. I compared three criteria in isolated runs; the selected criterion allowed training for three times longer before stopping.
  • Reevaluation: after the fixes, the network crossed the threshold on 23.7% of documents, up from 0.6%. Agreement with OCR moved from chance to moderate, and probability squared error fell below one quarter. I reran existing evaluation tools to revise the conclusion about the network’s contribution.

Architecture validation

Fine-tuning depth evaluated with 5-fold.

Compare fine-tuning depth

The training (97%) versus test (70%, 40 images) gap prompted a cross-validation comparison of three unfreezing depths.

With ImageNet weights, I compared head only, head + last block, and head + last two blocks. Protocol: stratified 5-fold on 406 training images, up to 30 epochs, patience 7, the same seed and class balancing.

84.2% ± 1.7 average validation accuracy of the selected configuration — the highest and most stable of the three
67.0% ± 3.9 accuracy for training only the classification head — lowest observed mean in this protocol
40 images in the test set that triggered the initial alarm — too much variance to support a conclusion on its own

Two unfrozen blocks: 84.2% ± 1.7, versus 67.0% ± 3.9 for the head alone and 74.9% ± 6.7 for one block. Higher mean and lower fold dispersion favor configuration C in this protocol; they do not prove configuration A lacks capacity. This study uses 406 training images and a historical 40-image test: it is not the 297/64/64 final benchmark split.

Engineering and security

Authentication and public-documentation limits.

Validation of identity, session, authorization, device, and biometric attempt.

In simple terms

Login generates a signed temporary credential; protected routes validate it before performing any action.

Login → validated credential → authorized access

FastAPI’s OAuth2PasswordBearer standardizes how the API receives the token. In this project, it does not represent social login through Google or Microsoft.

The public documentation summarizes the security controls. Implementation details require validation against the private code; legal compliance assessment remains outside this project.

Delivery integrity

Packaged-model traceability.

Audit checkpoint lineage

The delivery-image audit identified a PyTorch checkpoint that did not match the versioned checksum.

An experiment overwrote the promoted checkpoint. The packaged ONNX also differed from the versioned checkpoints, as shown by image-level probability comparisons.

Why historical metrics did not expose the issue

The recorded accuracies were not comparable: each training run used a different split (424/44 versus 297/64).

90.9% vs 78.1% → different splits → meaningless comparison

Evaluating both on the same test set exposed the actual difference — the delivery was serving the worse model.

The documented export command failed due to undeclared dependencies, leading to manual exports without traceability.

  • Release validation: the gate now checks checksums and aborts on mismatch.
  • Lineage: export records the checkpoint-to-ONNX link, verified at release.
  • Reproducibility: I declared dependencies and obtained two byte-identical exports.

The audit found 12 fewer correct predictions in the incorrect artifact (49/64 versus 61/64, an 18.75-point difference). This justifies checking the actually packaged model. These checkpoints and this audit are not the EfficientNet + Logistic Regression benchmark (56/64); 95.31% must not be advertised as that experiment’s selected-classifier performance.

Delivery benchmark

The multi-stage gain, without changing the runtime.

Isolate the multi-stage effect

I isolated the multi-stage effect in two ONNX images with the same code, model, and dependencies: direct installation in the final image or a separate build copying only the runtime.

32.9 MiB less (7.4%) is a modest packaging improvement with a fixed runtime. The historical ~94.6% inference-image reduction includes removing CUDA/PyTorch; it cannot be attributed solely to multi-stage builds.

Delivery trajectory

From 10.59 GB to 1.11 GB across releases.

Read image-size evolution

The manifest records image sizes per release. The series shows progression but does not isolate each change's effect.

~9.48 GB between the first delivery and the current one, both images combined
9.5× smaller overall; the inference image alone became 19× smaller
414 MB is what the client downloads today, with the images compressed into the package

10.59 → 1.11 GB means about 89.5% less total disk (9.48 GB from rounded values). Inference alone fell about 94.6%; these have different denominators. The largest drop came from the runtime; the next from the facial model. Compressed images (414 MB), installed size, and RAM are distinct measurements.

Architecture decision

CPU inference remains synchronous; asynchronous concurrency handles I/O waits.

Load testing revealed connections held during bcrypt, exhausting the pool. With hashes costing about 100 ms, each connection limited throughput to ten logins per second. The diagnosis indicated releasing connections before hashing.

Hardware constraint

The target server had no GPU.

Inspect disk, RAM, and ONNX parity

The target server had Intel HD 4600, 8 GB RAM, and no dedicated GPU. The initial image included about 6 GB of CUDA and cuDNN unused on that hardware.

I measured disk and memory separately. CUDA drove disk cost; in RAM, the facial package loaded five models to use two, replicated per server process.

−2 GB of RAM returned to the system, about one quarter of the machine
−95% in inference-image size, from 8.1 GB to 433 MB
0 classifier decisions changed when switching runtime

I migrated the classifier to ONNX Runtime. The export script compares runtimes on the held-out test and fails if any decision changes. Preprocessing was bit-identical, with no changed decisions.

Inference isolation

I retained triage in a separate service after measuring its processing cost.

The network took 14 ms and OCR took 909 ms (98% of processing time). Merging triage into the two-process backend would occupy half its capacity for about one second. A separate service preserves capacity for facial attendance.
